visuals.heading: Each Path Actually Leads

items.text: An MSCS deepens your technical skill and usually opens a faster route into strong-paying engineering roles abroad, at a lower total cost than an MBA abroad.

blocks.heading: Engineering Skill Is Still Your Strongest

items.text: Staying technical protects the specific skill the market is already paying you for, rather than trading it for a broader but less proven one.
You want the shortest path into a strong-paying technical role abroad

blocks.heading: Honest Case for Pivoting to Business

items.text: You have already tested that you enjoy the business side more than the build side
If a few years into your engineering job the parts you found most engaging were prioritization calls, stakeholder conversations, or business strategy, that is real evidence, not a guess.
Your target role genuinely needs the MBA credential and network, not just business knowledge
Burnout from a tough engineering job is a reason to look at your workload, manager, or team, not automatic proof that you want a career in business.
An MSCS is a strong move if you want to go deeper technically.

items.text: "MS is only for people who can't get into a good MBA programme."

"Any master's abroad guarantees a strong return."
Deeper technical specialization: systems, ML/AI, security, distributed computing, or a research-adjacent track.
Roles like software engineer, ML engineer, applied scientist, or platform/infra engineer, usually at a higher technical ceiling than a bachelor's-only hire.
A direct route into US or Canadian tech hiring, since most MSCS programmes are built around campus recruiting for engineering roles.
A narrower but deeper resume: the story is "I went deeper into the craft," not "I broadened my scope."
